issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette:
Boonsri Chaiyasit is a 52-year-old Thai American man who has been working as an HVAC technician for nearly two decades, a trade he came to with quiet pride, having built a reputation for reliability and precision across the commercial buildings and industrial facilities he services throughout the region. He is married and describes his wife, Nong, as the person most aware of how profoundly he has changed since the incident fourteen months ago. He presented for his initial intake visibly guarded, his shoulders drawn up, his hands rarely still, and with the particular exhaustion of a man who has not felt safe inside his own body for over a year.

The exposure occurred during a routine maintenance call at a food processing facility. Boonsri had been contracted to service the refrigeration and ventilation systems in a large cold-storage unit. What neither he nor the facility's management initially knew was that a corroded ammonia line had been leaking into the enclosed mechanical room for several hours before his arrival. Within minutes of entering the space, Boonsri began to feel a burning in his throat and eyes, then a tightening in his chest so severe he described it as being squeezed from the inside. He shouted for help but the door, which opened outward and had partially jammed against a shifted floor panel, did not yield immediately. He spent what he estimates was four to five minutes alone in that room, unable to breathe properly, certain he was dying. When a colleague finally wrenched the door open and pulled him out, Boonsri collapsed on the loading dock. He was hospitalized for three days with chemical burns to his airway and residual pulmonary inflammation.

In the weeks that followed his discharge, Boonsri returned to work cautiously, but the mechanical rooms and equipment corridors he had navigated for years had become something else entirely. The smell of any chemical agent - cleaning products, refrigerant, even certain industrial lubricants - could stop him mid-step, flooding him with a bodily certainty that something was wrong with the air around him, that the environment was quietly turning toxic. These were not abstract worries. They arrived as physical conviction, his chest tightening, his throat registering a phantom burn. On one occasion, a coworker used a solvent-based cleaner nearby and Boonsri walked off the job site without explanation. He had come to believe, in a way he found impossible to argue himself out of, that his body's alarm system was simply correct - that the danger was real and present even when others insisted otherwise. When his supervisor or Nong told him he was safe, he heard the words but felt nothing shift. The reassurance landed somewhere outside him, unable to reach whatever part of him had decided that trust was no longer affordable.

At home, the vigilance extended and deepened. Before bed each night, Boonsri checks the doors and windows repeatedly - the front door, the back door, the garage entry, the bedroom window - sometimes cycling through the sequence three or four times before he can lie down. He cannot fully account for what he is checking against, only that his body demands the confirmation. He keeps the bedroom door open so he can hear the house, and he has not been comfortable in any room alone for longer than a few minutes. If Nong leaves to run an errand, he finds reasons to go with her or he sits near the front window. The stillness of an empty room feels, to him, like the stillness of that mechanical space before the burning started.

He has quietly stopped accepting any job assignments to enclosed mechanical rooms, telling his dispatcher he prefers exterior and rooftop units. He avoids situations he anticipates might be stressful - he has declined family gatherings, skipped his nephew's graduation, and stopped watching the news. He has not attempted to relax deliberately, because the loosening of vigilance feels, in his own words, like turning your back on something that is still moving.

What finally brought Boonsri to seek help was a conversation with Nong in which she told him, gently but plainly, that she was frightened - not of him, but for him. What he most hopes for, he said quietly at the end of the intake, is to be able to walk into a room and simply be there.
